A2Eval: Agentic and Automated Evaluation for Embodied Brain

Shuai Zhang Affiliation: Zhejiang University, China Affiliation: Westlake University, China Affiliation: Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics, China Correspondence to: zhangshuai@westlake.edu.cn    Jiayu Hu Affiliation: Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics, China    Zijie Chen Affiliation: Westlake University, China    Zeyuan Ding Affiliation: Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics, China    Yi Zhang Affiliation: Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics, China    Yingji Zhang Affiliation: University of Manchester, UK    Ziyi Zhou Affiliation: Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics, China Affiliation: Southern University of Science and Technology, China    Junwei Liao Affiliation: Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics, China    Shengjie Zhou Affiliation: Xiamen University Malaysia, Malaysia    Yong Dai Affiliation: Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics, China    Zhenzhong Lan Affiliation: Westlake University, China    Xiaozhu Ju Affiliation: Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics, China
Abstract

Current embodied VLM evaluation relies on static, expert-defined, manually annotated benchmarks that exhibit severe redundancy and coverage imbalance. This labor‑intensive paradigm drains computational and annotation resources, inflates costs, and distorts model rankings, ultimately stifling iterative development. To address this, we propose Agentic Automatic Evaluation (A2Eval), the first agentic framework that automates benchmark curation and evaluation through two collaborative agents. The Data Agent autonomously induces capability dimensions and assembles a balanced, compact evaluation suite, while the Eval Agent synthesizes and validates executable evaluation pipelines, enabling fully autonomous, high-fidelity assessment. Evaluated across 10 benchmarks and 13 models, A2Eval compresses evaluation suites by 85%, reduces overall computational costs by 77%, and delivers a 4.6×\times speedup while preserving evaluation quality. Crucially, A2Eval corrects systematic ranking biases, improves human alignment to Spearman’s ρ=0.85\rho=0.85, and maintains high ranking fidelity (Kendall’s τ=0.81\tau=0.81), establishing a new standard for high-fidelity, low-cost embodied assessment. Our code and data will be public soon.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Evaluating modern embodied vision-language models (VLM) has become the “compass” for navigating the rapid advancements in Embodied AI (Liu et al., 2025; Cong and Mo, 2025). A comprehensive and precise evaluation mechanism is not only a benchmark for academic breakthroughs but also a cornerstone for industrial decision-making (Yifan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). However, the cost of this “compass” is becoming prohibitive: evaluating a single model across fragmented benchmarks now consumes over 3200 GPU hours (see Table 5), creating a significant financial and computational burden that stifles iterative research.

This crisis stems from a Broken Evaluation Ecosystem rooted in the labor-intensive “expert definition + manual annotation” paradigm. As shown in Figure 1(a) and 3, current benchmarks exhibit up to 92% sample similarity and severe capacity distribution skew. Critical reasoning capacity like PhysCausal constitute less examples, while easy-to-annotate tasks dominate. This creates a “lose-lose” dilemma characterized by three systemic pathologies: (1) Coverage Imbalance & Redundancy: Massive sample duplication and skewed task distribution lead to repetitive, unbalanced assessments that fail to comprehensively evaluate model capabilities. (2) Ranking Distortion: Models overfit to overrepresented tasks appear top-ranked despite critical weaknesses, distorting leaderboards and misleading research directions. (3) Prohibitive Evaluation Cost: The combination of evaluating massive redundant samples and manually constructing inference and scoring logic for each benchmark creates substantial computational and human effort overhead, making evaluation cycles slow and costly, stifling iterative development.

To resolve these tensions, we propose Agentic and Automatic Evaluation (A2Eval), a paradigm shift that treats benchmark curation as an optimization problem: maximize capability coverage and diversity while minimizing redundancy and human effort. A2Eval replaces the traditional paradigm with a fully autonomous process via two collaborative agents:

Data Agent addresses Coverage Imbalance, Redundancy, and Ranking Distortion by autonomously inferring capability dimensions—eliminating reliance on subjective expert definitions. By automatically inducing capability dimensions and performing diversity-aware sampling, it constructs a balanced, compact evaluation suite that substantially reduces benchmark size and redundant computation while maintaining comprehensive capacity coverage, thereby correcting systematic ranking biases and significantly lowering evaluation cost.

Eval Agent resolves the Manual Pipeline Bottleneck by automatically synthesizing and validating executable evaluation pipelines. Through iterative sandbox refinement of both inference and scoring logic, it enables fully autonomous, high-fidelity evaluation without manual intervention.

Extensive experiments across 10 benchmarks and 13 models demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Our main contributions are summarised as follows:

(1) First Agentic Evaluation Framework: We present the first fully automated evaluation framework that decouples assessment from static expert labels, replacing manual processes with a scalable, autonomous agentic system that addresses both benchmark construction and execution challenges.

(2) Balanced and Compact Benchmark Construction: Our Data Agent corrects Coverage Imbalance and Ranking Distortion, filters 85% redundant samples, boosts human preference alignment to 0.85 (Spearman’s ρ\rho), and reduces overall cost by 77% with 4.6×\times evaluation throughput acceleration.

(3) Autonomous Executable Evaluation Pipeline: Our Eval Agent automatically constructs validated inference and scoring logic, achieving 96.9% fidelity while enabling fully autonomous evaluation without manual intervention.

2 Related Work

2.1 Embodied Reasoning Benchmarks

Recent benchmarks evaluate a wide range of embodied reasoning capabilities. Tasks such as Where2Place (Yuan et al., 2025) and VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025a) target placement and spatial understanding, while RefSpatial (Zhou et al., 2025), RoboSpatial (Song et al., 2025), EmbSpatial (Du et al., 2024), and OmniSpatial (Jia et al., 2025) extend spatial reasoning to grounding and manipulation. ERQA (Team et al., 2025b) and COSMOS (Azzolini et al., 2025) focus on physical and causal reasoning, whereas BLINK (Fu et al., 2024) and EgoSchema (Mangalam et al., 2023) assess multi-modal perception and egocentric understanding. Recent vision–language models (e.g., Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025a), InternVL3.5 (Wang et al., 2025)) and embodied-specialized systems (e.g., Pelican-VL (Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025b), RoboBrain (Team et al., 2025a)) increasingly incorporate such benchmarks, alongside system-level frameworks like EmbodiedBench (Yang et al., 2025b) and EAI (Li et al., 2024). However, the rapid proliferation of benchmarks introduces evaluation challenges, including substantial redundancy (Zhang et al., 2025d) and high computational cost, particularly for long video-based benchmarks (Mangalam et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025a).

2.2 Agentic Evaluation and Benchmarks

Parallel efforts have explored automated benchmark construction. Code2Bench (Zhang et al., 2025c) and OKBench (Li et al., 2025) provide domain-specific pipelines for generating new benchmarks with contamination control and reproducibility protocols. However, these methods focus on creating fresh evaluation sets rather than consolidating existing heterogeneous benchmarks or addressing redundancy and computational costs. Our work differs from prior work by introducing (1) automatic capability induction with balanced sampling across domains, (2) redundancy-aware benchmark consolidation, and (3) a unified end-to-end data and evaluation pipeline.

3 Method

We propose Agentic Automatic Evaluation (A2Eval) to address the challenges of benchmark redundancy, fragmented coverage, and high evaluation costs in embodied domains. As shown in Figure 2, A2Eval is a two-agent framework that automates the complete evaluation lifecycle from benchmark construction to model assessment. It consists of a Data Agent (Section 3.1), which discovers unified capability dimensions through specialized agent collaboration (Proposer, Reviewer, and Assigner) and constructs a compact, balanced benchmark through the Assigner’s dimension assignment and diversity-aware sampling, and an Eval Agent (Section 3.2), which generates executable evaluation pipelines through iterative code synthesis. For detailed algorithmic procedures and prompt designs, refer to Appendix C.

3.1 Data Agent

The Data Agent constructs a capability-aware, low-redundancy, and balanced benchmark for a target domain given existing benchmark information pools ℬ={Bi}i=1NB\mathcal{B}=\{B_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{B}} and their example sets ℰ=⋃i=1NBEi\mathcal{E}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{N_{B}}E_{i}, where NBN_{B} is the number of benchmarks. The core innovation lies in treating benchmark construction as a two-stage agentic workflow: (i) Dimension Induction, where multiple specialized agents collaboratively discover a unified capability taxonomy, and (ii) Benchmark Construction, where the Assigner performs dimension assignment and diversity-aware sampling to produce a balanced, non-redundant test set that preserves comprehensive semantic coverage.

Dimension Induction.

Dimension induction operates through iterative collaboration among three specialized agents with distinct roles and reasoning capabilities: a Proposer 𝒜p\mathcal{A}_{p} that generates candidate capability dimensions, a Reviewer 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} that critiques proposals from coverage, independence and balance perspectives, and an Assigner 𝒜a\mathcal{A}_{a} that reports dimension balance through example assignment and diversity-aware sampling. These agents communicate through a shared memory MM that records historical proposals and critiques, enabling collective reasoning toward an optimal dimension set.

At iteration ii, the Proposer generates a candidate dimension set Di+1D_{i+1} by reasoning over benchmark information ℬ\mathcal{B}, the Reviewer’s critique CiC_{i}, and historical memory MM:

Di+1=𝒜p​(ℬ,Ci,M).D_{i+1}=\mathcal{A}_{p}(\mathcal{B},C_{i},M). (1)

The Proposer refines dimensions based on specific feedback from CiC_{i} while incorporating experience from MM.

The Reviewer evaluates Di+1D_{i+1} along three criteria: (a) conceptual redundancy among dimensions, (b) coverage comprehensiveness relative to domain requirements, and (c) dimension balance. The critique Ci+1C_{i+1} is produced by:

Ci+1=𝒜r​(Di+1,S(r)).C_{i+1}=\mathcal{A}_{r}(D_{i+1},S^{(r)}). (2)

where S(r)S^{(r)} contains balance statistics from the Assigner. The memory is updated as M←M∪{(Di+1,Ci+1)}M\leftarrow M\cup\{(D_{i+1},C_{i+1})\} after each iteration.

The Proposer and Reviewer iterate until dimensions stabilize (Di+1=DiD_{i+1}=D_{i}), producing candidate D(r+1)D^{(r+1)}. To validate balance, D(r+1)D^{(r+1)} is tested through actual example assignment and sampling by the Assigner, yielding balance statistics S(r+1)S^{(r+1)}. The Reviewer incorporates this empirical evidence into its next critique, triggering dimension refinement (e.g., merging under-represented dimensions). This agent-driven validation loop continues until producing a stable dimension set DD.

Benchmark Construction.

Given the validated dimension set DD, the Assigner constructs the benchmark through a two-stage process: dimension assignment followed by diversity-aware sampling. This transforms the dimension taxonomy into an actual test set that eliminates redundancy while preserving comprehensive capability coverage.

Dimension Assignment. The Assigner employs an ensemble of NvN_{v} voter agents {𝒜a1,…,𝒜aNv}\{\mathcal{A}_{a}^{1},\dots,\mathcal{A}_{a}^{N_{v}}\} that independently reason about capability requirements. Each voter 𝒜ak\mathcal{A}_{a}^{k} analyzes example ej∈ℰe_{j}\in\mathcal{E} and produces dimension assignment Dj​kD_{jk} based on its interpretation. The final assignment DjD_{j} emerges from majority consensus:

Dj=MajorityVote​({Dj​k}k=1Nv).D_{j}=\text{MajorityVote}\big(\{D_{jk}\}_{k=1}^{N_{v}}\big). (3)

Per-dimension example pools are aggregated as

Edk={ej∈ℰ:dk∈Dj}E_{d_{k}}=\{e_{j}\in\mathcal{E}:d_{k}\in D_{j}\} (4)

for each dk∈Dd_{k}\in D.

Diversity-Aware Sampling. Following dimension assignment, the Assigner performs diversity-aware sampling to eliminate intra-dimension redundancy while preserving semantic diversity through clustering-based selection. For each dimension dkd_{k}, examples e∈Edke\in E_{d_{k}} are embedded as x=Encoder​(e)x=\text{Encoder}(e) into a semantic space. If |Edk|<K|E_{d_{k}}|<K, all examples are retained; otherwise, we select the example closest to each of the KK cluster centroids μj\mu_{j}:

Edks={arg⁡minx∈Cj​‖x−μj‖}j=1K.E_{d_{k}}^{\mathrm{s}}=\big\{\arg\min_{x\in C_{j}}\|x-\mu_{j}\|\big\}_{j=1}^{K}. (5)

This centroid-based selection ensures that retained examples EdksE_{d_{k}}^{\mathrm{s}} sparsely yet strategically cover the semantic manifold (visualized in Figure 4.2), removing redundancy without sacrificing representation completeness. By applying uniform KK across dimensions, cross-dimension balance is achieved while each dimension maintains maximal internal diversity. The final benchmark is constructed as:

ℰs=⋃k=1NdEdks.\mathcal{E}^{\text{s}}=\bigcup_{k=1}^{N_{d}}E_{d_{k}}^{\mathrm{s}}. (6)

with balance statistics

S={|Edks|:dk∈D}.S=\{|E_{d_{k}}^{\text{s}}|:d_{k}\in D\}. (7)

3.2 Eval Agent

The Eval Agent executes automated evaluation on the benchmark produced by the Data Agent. It consists of two specialized roles: (i) an Evaluator that constructs model inference logic, and (ii) a Scorer that constructs performance assessment logic. These roles collaborate with a sandbox executor to iteratively generate and validate a complete evaluation pipeline.

Model Inference Logic Construction.

The Evaluator 𝒜e\mathcal{A}_{e} synthesizes inference logic that integrates the target model MM with benchmark test examples 𝒯\mathcal{T} sampled from ℰs\mathcal{E}^{\text{s}}. At iteration ii, the Evaluator generates executable inference code FieF_{i}^{e} that implements: loading test inputs, invoking MM, and producing model predictions.

The sandbox executor 𝒳\mathcal{X} runs FieF_{i}^{e} on model MM with test cases 𝒯\mathcal{T}. If execution succeeds, the validated logic Fe=FieF^{e}=F_{i}^{e} is finalized. Otherwise, 𝒳\mathcal{X} returns diagnostic feedback EiE_{i} to the Evaluator to update inference logic:

Fi+1e=𝒜e​(M,𝒯,Fie,Ei).F_{i+1}^{e}=\mathcal{A}_{e}(M,\mathcal{T},F_{i}^{e},E_{i}). (8)

This synthesis-validation loop iterates until FeF^{e} executes reliably or reaches a predefined iteration budget. The resulting artifact FeF^{e} constitutes the validated inference logic for systematic model evaluation.

Model Scoring Logic Construction.

Given the validated inference logic FeF^{e} and the model predictions 𝒫𝒯=Fe​(M,𝒯)\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{T}}=F^{e}(M,\mathcal{T}) it produces on test cases 𝒯\mathcal{T}, the Scorer 𝒜s\mathcal{A}_{s} synthesizes evaluation logic to assess model performance. At iteration jj, the Scorer generates executable scoring code FjsF_{j}^{s} conditioned on the test cases 𝒯\mathcal{T} and model outputs 𝒫𝒯\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{T}}:

The sandbox executor 𝒳\mathcal{X} runs FjsF_{j}^{s} on the test outputs 𝒫𝒯\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{T}}. If execution succeeds and produces valid metrics, the logic Fs=FjsF^{s}=F_{j}^{s} is finalized. Otherwise, 𝒳\mathcal{X} returns diagnostic feedback EjE_{j} to the Scorer, triggering iterative refinement:

Fj+1s=𝒜s​(𝒯,𝒫𝒯,Fjs,Ej).F_{j+1}^{s}=\mathcal{A}_{s}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{T}},F_{j}^{s},E_{j}). (9)

The synthesis-validation loop continues until FsF^{s} executes reliably or reaches the iteration budget. The resulting artifact FsF^{s} constitutes reproducible scoring logic for comprehensive model assessment.

Benchmark Evaluation Execution.

Once both inference logic FeF^{e} and scoring logic FsF^{s} are validated, the complete evaluation pipeline is executed on the constructed benchmark ℰs\mathcal{E}^{\text{s}}. The Evaluator applies FeF^{e} to generate model predictions for all test cases:

𝒫=Fe​(M,ℰs),\mathcal{P}=F^{e}(M,\mathcal{E}^{\text{s}}), (10)

and the Scorer applies FsF^{s} to compute final evaluation metrics:

Results=Fs​(ℰs,𝒫).\text{Results}=F^{s}(\mathcal{E}^{\text{s}},\mathcal{P}). (11)

This produces comprehensive assessment results for the target model MM across all capability dimensions in DD.

4 Experiments

We evaluate A2Eval in the embodied vision–language reasoning domain, where models must jointly perform perception, spatial reasoning, physical understanding, and multi-step decision making over visual inputs. We validate that our Data Agent produces semantically meaningful capability dimensions and balanced benchmarks, aligning with human judgment rankings. Moreover, we highlight that our approach significantly improves evaluation efficiency, while the Eval Agent achieves high accuracy in automated inference and scoring. Together, these results demonstrate that A2Eval enables fully automated, efficient, and trustworthy capability-aware evaluation.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks.

We focus on the embodied vision–language reasoning domain and adopt ten established benchmarks, compromising COSMOS (Azzolini et al., 2025), ERQA (Team et al., 2025b), Where2Place (Yuan et al., 2025), VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025a), OmniSpatial (Jia et al., 2025), EgoSchema (Mangalam et al., 2023), BLINK (Fu et al., 2024), RefSpatial (Zhou et al., 2025), RoboSpatial (Song et al., 2025), and EmbSpatial (Du et al., 2024). These datasets both inform benchmark construction via the Data Agent and serve as reference corpora for analyzing redundancy, coverage, and evaluation efficiency. Detailed information on these benchmarks and their redundancy examples is provided in Appendix A.

Models.

We evaluate a diverse set of vision language models with different scales and architectures, including several Qwen2.5-VL models (Bai et al., 2025b), multiple InternVL-3.5 variants (Wang et al., 2025), the latest Qwen3-VL series (Bai et al., 2025a), as well as the GPT-5 Mini as a closed-source model. All evaluations are performed with a batch size of 1 using the lmms-eval framework (Zhang et al., 2024).

Evaluation Settings.

By default, large-scale models (e.g., Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Thinking) are deployed with the vLLM backend, while smaller models (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct) utilize the PyTorch backend with 8-way data parallelism via Accelerate. We apply greedy decoding for all models to ensure deterministic outputs. Video inputs are uniformly sampled to 32 frames at 2 FPS, and the maximum generation length is set to 4096 tokens. More details are provided in Appendix B.

A2Eval Setup.

For the agentic workflow, we employ GPT-4o as the Assigner, while the Proposer, Reviewer, and Eval Agents are implemented using Gemini 3 Pro. In the Assigner’s diversity-aware sampling for the Data Agent, examples are encoded by concatenating visual and textual embeddings. Textual content is embedded using a sentence representation model11 1 https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, while visual representations are extracted using CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). For video inputs, 32 uniformly sampled frames are processed, with the final visual embedding obtained by averaging their frame-level CLIP features. The number of clusters KK is set to 500 across all dimensions to strike a balance between semantic coverage and evaluation efficiency.

4.2 Overall Results

Unified Dimensions.

Our Data Agent automatically induces eight capability dimensions for embodied visual–language reasoning. Table 1 lists each induced dimension with a concise abbreviation and the full definition produced by the agent.

Balanced Benchmark.

Table 2 reports the number of examples assigned to each dimension and retained after Assigner’s diversity-aware sampling. The “Other” category is omitted due to negligible size. The raw pool contains 24,519 examples, while the sampled benchmark contains 3,781 examples.

Coverage and Diversity.

Figure 1(a) visualizes how original benchmarks distribute across dimensions. Benchmarks emphasize distinct capabilities, with substantial overlap across dimensions. This reveals that aggregating existing benchmarks provides broad but redundant coverage, motivating capability-aware consolidation rather than simple union. Figure 4.2 shows UMAP (McInnes et al., 2018) projections of sample embeddings for two representative dimensions: PercepObj and SpatGeo (others are listed in Figure 5). Our selected subset (marked with “+” symbols) sparsely yet strategically covers the full semantic manifold, demonstrating that our Data Agent preserves comprehensive capability coverage while removing intra-dimension redundancy.
